transcript:
Meeting header:
- Date: 2025-11-04
- Time: 15:00 PST
- Duration: ~46 minutes
- Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Ethan Cho (Redwood SE), Lina Gomez (Redwood CSM); Rajesh Kumar (AtlasFin lead ML), Sofia Alvarez (PM), Ben Li (backend), Hannah Park (security)

[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick agenda: check results from your staging runs, walk through the SDK function/tool calling flow, and structured output issues. Is that still good?
[00:12] Rajesh: Yep, good. we've got some logs ready. sorry for a tiny delay on the harness, had to re-run a couple jobs.
[00:20] Ethan: no worries. quick note: i'll show the snippet that we recommend for strict schema enforcement, and then we can look at the failure modes you saw.
[00:30] Sofia: one ask from product — we need deterministic JSON outputs for downstream ingestion. any hallucinated fields break downstream pipelines.
[00:40] Ethan: understood. so two approaches we've seen work: one is SDK function-calling mode where you declare functions and the model returns a call, and the other is structured_output / response_format where the model returns a JSON schema. Both have trade-offs.
[00:58] Ben: in our runs, when streaming is enabled we sometimes get partial chunks and the JSON parser fails, so our consumer crashes. we saw like 8% error rate on the first 5k requests.
[01:12] Ethan: yeah streaming + strict JSON is tricky — you need a replay/reassembly layer on the client to stitch chunks before parsing, or use function-calling which is typically returned as a single call object in the final message. streaming helps latency but increases handling complexity.
[01:30] Rajesh: also noticed that when we enforce the json_schema in structured_output, p95 latency increased from ~320ms to ~370ms on your hosted pool. is that expected?
[01:45] Maya: rough numbers — structured validation can add some compute overhead, and if you force multiple sampling passes to conform, it may add tokens. the p95 bump you mentioned is in line with what we've measured for similar workloads. i think Ethan has the benchmark details.
[02:00] Ethan: i do — i shared a small CSV in the slack thread and i'll upload it to the shared drive after the call. the trade-off is: stricter outputs reduce downstream parsing errors but you pay a latency and sometimes token-cost premium. we saw ~12-18% token overhead depending on prompt design.
[02:18] Sofia: token cost matters. can we do a hybrid where only certain fields are enforced strictly and others are more flexible?
[02:26] Ethan: yes, recommend a schema that marks critical fields as required and optional fields as permissive. also use a guardrail layer: attempt parsing, and if parsing fails, fall back to a tolerance mode that extracts by regex or runs a small rerun with a focused prompt.
[02:42] Ben: ok. about function/tool calls — when the model returns a function name, we route to our internal service. but sometimes the model invents a function name that doesn't exist and we hit a 404 in our router. any best practice?
[02:58] Ethan: two options: whitelist functions in the SDK function registry so the model only sees available names, or use the SDK's 'tooling manifest' so that unrecognized calls are rejected at the SDK layer. we have an example where the SDK returns a deterministic enum of allowed tools.
[03:15] Rajesh: we did whitelist, but the model still sometimes tries close variants — e.g., 'get_account_bal' instead of 'get_account_balance'. spelling errors.
[03:26] Ethan: that's typical. set up a mapping table and canonicalization step in your router. also, using a higher temperature for calls can increase creative variants; set temperature to 0–0.2 for function selection to reduce that.
[03:40] Hannah: security question — if we use Redwood Dedicated or a private deploy, how does function calling interact with our VPC? we want tool calls to only hit internal endpoints.
[03:52] Maya: good question. on Dedicated or Private, you can configure the routing policy so tool calls map to internal hostnames, and the control plane won't leak payloads. also KMS integration for secrets is supported. we'll include the network diagram in the security pack.
[04:08] Hannah: perfect. please share SOC2 details — we still need confirmation on audit logs and retention.
[04:15] Lina: noted, we'll send the security pack after this call. link: https://redwood.example/security-pack (we'll send actual PDF).
[04:24] Ben: back to streaming — we attempted to buffer until the final token, but some timeouts caused early parsing. any best practices on timeouts?
[04:36] Ethan: client-side timeout should be higher than worst-case p95. if you need low latency, consider a small partial-parse strategy that marks responses 'incomplete' and queues for background reconciliation. also, the SDK has a 'finalize_on_end' flag that helps only return complete function objects.
[04:54] Rajesh: what about KV cache interactions? we saw that cached prefixes sometimes returned stale tool responses.
[05:03] Ethan: that sounds like prefix caching being too aggressive. set the cache TTL lower for tool-invocation prompts or disable prefix caching for prompts where you expect real-time data. we'll share config snippets.
[05:18] Maya: quick demo time — Ethan, can you share the snippet for structured_output v2 that you mentioned?
[05:24] Ethan: sure — (screen) okay, here's an example. i won't paste all code, but gist: define schema (fields, types, required), pass to SDK call as structured_output: {schema: ..., mode: "enforce"}. There's also an alternative mode "soft" which only validates but doesn't force rerolls.
[05:44] (transcription: faint typing)
[05:52] Ethan: important caveat — enforce mode may trigger additional retries if the model doesn't match, which increases tokens. soft mode logs violations in telemetry for later processing.
[06:08] Sofia: can telemetry give us per-field failure rates? that'll help prioritize which fields to enforce.
[06:16] Ethan: yes — we can include per-field validation metrics in the benchmark CSV. we'll add a column for failure_type and field_name.
[06:26] Rajesh: on our runs, the top failure was missing 'transaction_id' in 3.7% of responses, then malformed 'amount' string in 1.1%. the rest are small.
[06:38] Ethan: for transaction_id i'd mark as required and maybe include an explicit example in the prompt to bias generation. also consider adding a synthetic post-processing check that discards outputs without transaction_id and triggers a safe fallback.
[06:52] Ben: another practical: our backend is Java-based and the JSON parser is strict. any library suggestions to do streaming-safe parsing? we use Jackson.
[07:02] Ethan: Jackson is fine if you feed it complete JSON. for streaming assemble at the SDK boundary then hand over complete JSON. or use a forgiving parser for partials then re-validate. we'll add a sample reassembly middleware for Node/Python/Java in the repo.
[07:20] Rajesh: about latency — you mentioned Dedicated pool for canary. how much improvement should we expect?
[07:28] Maya: Dedicated removes noisy neighbors and gives predictable throughput. for this workload we expect p95 to drop by ~20–30% vs shared hosted at similar model/sequence lengths, depending on instance type. exact numbers in the CSV.
[07:40] Sofia: cost — dedicated is more fixed commit pricing; we need a calculator for expected unit cost vs hosted.
[07:46] Maya: yes, we'll share a simple TCO calc. Ethan, can you produce a per-1k token cost estimate from the benchmark?
[07:53] Ethan: yep. i'll include per-request token counts and cost envelope.
[07:58] Hannah: one more security thing — audit logs. if a function call includes PII, is there field-level redaction?
[08:06] Ethan: on Private and Dedicated you control the logging level; agents can redact at the SDK before sending. Redwood can also support automated field redaction for known PII fields via the ingest pipeline — that's in the security pack.
[08:18] Sofia: ok, to recap, we want strict schema on transaction_id, soft validation for others, implement reassembly middleware, and run a canary on Dedicated.
[08:28] Maya: correct. Lina will send the security pack and we'll share SDK snippets. Ben will implement the buffer middleware. Rajesh will run the harness.
[08:36] Rajesh: quick note — there was one weird error where the model returned a function call with an empty args object. caused a downstream NPE.
[08:46] Ethan: we log that as a function-call with missing args; best practice is to validate args shape before routing. if empty, return a 400 to caller and avoid executing. also try a 2nd micro-call to ask the model to fill missing args — sometimes a tiny clarifying follow-up fixes it.
[09:02] Ben: makes sense. i'll add validations.
[09:06] (brief cross-talk and typing)
[09:20] Maya: ok last items — deliverables and owners are in the action items. anything else?
[09:28] Sofia: timeline: if we can get the SDK code this week, we can aim to do the canary next week.
[09:34] Maya: sounds good. we'll target that. thanks everyone.
[09:40] (meeting ends)

Notes on transcription quality: some product names were auto-transcribed (e.g., "Redwood Dedicate" instead of "Dedicated"), occasional mis-heard acronyms (K V cache / KV cache). There are minor filler words and run-ons.
